newsitem.title: CYPRUS: British envoy expects direct talks on Cyprus.
newsitem.headline: British envoy expects direct talks on Cyprus.

text.p: A British envoy said on Friday it was just a matter of time before Greek and Turkish Cypriots started direct negotiations to resolve the dispute that has split Cyprus since 1974.

"I'd say the question is no longer whether, but when face-to-face negotiations will take place in a new, serious effort to find a comprehensive solution to the Cyprus problem," said Sir David Hannay, Britain's special envoy for Cyprus.

Leaders of the two communities, divided since a Turkish invasion of the northern third of the island in 1974 after a coup sponsored by the military government then ruling Greece, have not met since October 1994.

Hannay, ending a three-day visit to the Mediterranean island in which he had two meetings with Greek Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides and Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash, said it was up to the United Nations secretary-general to decide when to call the two sides to talks.
Britain has expressed hope that negotiations could get off the ground during the first half of the year.
Hannay said he had not detected a significant shift in positions but had not expected this in the preparatory stage.

"It is very clear that neither party will reach a settlement which is meaningful without a clear view of some of the detail and of the obligations of the parties under the agreement," he told a news conference at an abandoned hotel in the U.N.-controlled buffer zone splitting the capital Nicosia.
Hannay, whose second meetings with Clerides and Denktash on Thursday were under a press blackout, gave no specifics.
"There is obviously no point in underestimating the scale and nature of the task that lies ahead or hyping the prospects of success...that is not sensible," he said.

"There have been far too many failures in the past to simply brush aside the problems that obviously are still there. But I do believe that the chances of getting a settlement are better than they have been for quite a long time and I think they are also better than prospectively in the future one can see them being if this opportunity is not taken."
The Greek Cypriot-led government in the south is internationally recognised as legitimate. The breakaway Turkish Cypriot state created in 1983 is recognised only by Ankara.
U.N. attempts to reunite the island, a British colony until 1960, as a bicommunal, bizonal federation have floundered.
Fresh proximity talks began under U.N. auspices on Monday in an attempt to find common ground that could lead to direct negotiations.

Hannay said tension created earlier this year after the Greek Cypriots signed a deal with Russia for the supply of anti-aircraft missiles, and Turkey's response that it would use force to block their deployment, had not helped the atmosphere.
He also referred to the deaths last year of Greek Cypriot demonstrators during protests along the ceasefire line.

"In a sense it is the existence of this tension and the worsening of it which explains why the international community attaches such high importance to making a further serious and substantial, and I hope sucessful, effort to solve this problem," he said.
